[SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) uses causal, softmax-normalized attention over historical positions; [SHAN](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2018/0546.pdf) first pools long-term items with user-conditioned attention, then attends over that representation and short-term items. Neither explicitly preserves absolute evidence counts. Mathematically, repeated identical keys/values can increase their relative attention mass against other items, but duplicating the entire collection leaves normalized pooling unchanged when logits/values are unchanged. Position encodings complicate this invariance in SASRec. Thus attention can reflect repetition without providing a count-preserving accumulator; deduplicated item sets discard multiplicity altogether.

[HyperHawkes](https://pintonos.github.io/publication/peintner-www-2025/peintner-www-2025.pdf) explicitly models repeated latent intents using hypergraphs, soft clustering, and temporal Hawkes processes, alongside short-term attention. Its Hawkes formulation sums historical triggering contributions rather than normalizing them to unit mass, preserving cumulative support subject to temporal kernels. This concerns recurring intents across sessions, not simply repeated item IDs; it does not establish that an embedding-similarity residual measures recurrence.

Recommended controls, rather than claimed published ablations: compare the same residual using recent-only history, strictly disjoint older history, and full history; compare occurrence-level softmax/mean pooling, deduplicated pooling, and explicit frequency-weighted or unnormalized sums. Frequency-weighted means retain relative frequencies but still lose absolute count scale. Match windows, parameter counts, tuning budgets, and residual norms; otherwise gains may reflect scale or capacity. Hold recent context fixed while removing or duplicating older supporting evidence, and stratify validation gains by older support count while controlling recency and popularity. On Amazon, verify whether repetition means item recurrence or similarity among distinct items. Recent-only gains support a recency explanation; recurrence attribution requires incremental benefit from older evidence and sensitivity to its multiplicity.
